subject: spanish
title: Ask where something is—and check the directions
scene: You are looking for a pharmacy. A stranger gives you two directions. Let’s make the request, hear the answer, and confirm the turn before walking away.
goal: Ask for a place and understand recto, derecha and izquierda.
needs: Recognize estoy and a polite question. We will learn the direction phrases as whole expressions.
terms: Where is…? for the place we ask about here.
A la derecha / a la izquierda
To the right / to the left.
Next to the bank; de + el becomes del.
explanation: Suppose you can see the street but cannot find the pharmacy. ¿Dónde está la farmacia? is enough. Dónde means where, está is the form of estar we need for the pharmacy, and la farmacia supplies the place. Compare estoy en la farmacia: that says where I am. Changing the person or thing we are talking about changes estoy to está here.

The stranger replies Siga recto y gire a la derecha. There are two instructions: keep going straight, then turn right. Learn siga recto and gire a la derecha together before studying command endings. These are polite forms addressed to one person; a friend might say sigue and gira instead. If you caught only the turn, repeat it as a question: ¿A la derecha? That short check can save you a long walk in the wrong direction.
decision: Ask for one place, listen for the turn, then confirm that turn. If the answer is still unclear, use the slower-repeat request from the previous lesson. There is no prize for pretending to have understood.

mistake.attempt: The speaker said izquierda, but I heard a direction word, so I’ll turn right.
mistake.diagnosis: Derecha and izquierda lead in opposite directions. Recognizing that a word is a direction is not enough to choose the turn.
mistake.repair: Repeat the part you need checked: ¿A la izquierda? When the speaker confirms, turn left. You can also ask ¿Puede mostrarme?—Can you show me?—if pointing would help.
mistake.check: Point left and right as you say izquierda and derecha. Connect each word to the movement, rather than only to an English translation.

examples.title: Finding the pharmacy
examples.problem: Ask where the pharmacy is. The answer tells you to go straight, turn right, and look next to the bank.
steps: Use the place name after dónde está. You are asking about its location, not describing what kind of place it is.
Siga recto y gire a la derecha.
Siga recto: keep going straight. Y: and. Gire a la derecha: turn right.
A short rising question is enough to confirm the word you heard.
Sí. Está al lado del banco.
The pharmacy is next to the bank. Al lado de means next to; de el contracts to del.
examples.notice: You did not need a long reply. A precise check of the turn made the directions usable.

examples.title: The restaurant is on the other side
examples.problem: You hear El restaurante está a la izquierda. Which way should you look?
steps: The speaker is talking about the restaurant.
It is to the left. This is a location statement, not a command to turn at an unspecified future corner.
Repeat left, not the whole sentence, if that is the part you need checked.
examples.notice: A direction can describe where something is or tell you how to move. Listen to the whole phrase.

rescue: Use your hands: recto points forward, derecha points right, izquierda points left. Then hear the pharmacy answer again and follow the two movements in order.
transfer: Ask where the restaurant is, then check that it is on the left.
¿Dónde está el restaurante? ¿A la izquierda? The first question requests the location; the second confirms the direction.

questions.prompt: The answer says gire a la derecha. What should you do?
feedback: Left is izquierda.
Gire is the turn instruction; derecha gives right.
Recto means straight; this instruction includes a turn.
questions.hint: Attach derecha to a physical direction.
questions.nudge: Which direction did you point while saying derecha?

questions.prompt: You caught the directions but are unsure which turn was named. What is a useful reply?
choices: Repeat the uncertain direction as a question.
Say sí and choose at random.
Start conjugating every verb in the answer.
feedback: ¿A la derecha? checks the exact part that matters.
That leaves the uncertainty unresolved.
You can confirm the direction without producing a verb table.
questions.nudge: What would let the other person correct a misunderstanding?

subject: spanish
title: Make a plan without agreeing to the wrong day
scene: A friend invites you for coffee on Saturday, but you are free on Sunday. Let’s accept the idea while changing the day and settling a time.
goal: Invite a friend, say when you are unavailable, and agree on a day and time.
needs: Use puedo for I can and recognize a simple question. This exchange is between friends using tú forms.
terms: Do you want…? addressed to one familiar person.
I would like to; a useful polite phrase here.
explanation: ¿Quieres tomar un café el sábado? means Do you want to have a coffee on Saturday? Quieres is addressed to your friend. Compare quiero: I want. Tomar stays unchanged after quieres, just as comer stayed unchanged after quiero in the lunch lesson. Tomar un café is a normal way to say have a coffee; translating tomar as take in every sentence would make this sound stranger than it is.

You like the invitation, but Saturday does not work. Separate those facts: Me gustaría, pero no puedo el sábado. I’d like to, but I can’t on Saturday. Pero is but; it joins the interest and the difficulty. Then offer an alternative. When your friend asks ¿Y el domingo?—And Sunday?—El domingo sí answers the availability question already in the conversation. You can finish with ¿A las once? to propose eleven.
decision: Respond to both parts of the invitation: the activity and the date. Saying no to Saturday need not reject the coffee. Once you agree on Sunday, add a time so neither person has to guess what was settled.

mistake.attempt: I want to meet on Sunday, so I’ll answer sí to the Saturday invitation and explain later.
mistake.diagnosis: The friend may reasonably think Saturday is agreed. Interest in the activity and availability on the proposed day are different pieces of information.
mistake.repair: Me gustaría, pero no puedo el sábado. ¿El domingo? This accepts the idea and proposes a different day. Then check the time: ¿A las once?
mistake.check: Read the finished exchange and name the agreed day and time. They should be Sunday and eleven, not Saturday and an unspecified hour.

examples.title: Move the coffee to Sunday
examples.problem: A friend proposes Saturday. You prefer Sunday at eleven.
steps: Your friend proposes both an activity and a day.
Keep the interest; change the date
Me gustaría, pero no puedo el sábado.
Me gustaría acknowledges that you would like to. No puedo el sábado explains the scheduling problem.
And Sunday? — Sunday works. The short answer makes sense because availability is already the subject.
At eleven? — Perfect. You have now agreed on more than a vague intention to meet.
examples.notice: A clear reply can be brief. It only needs to settle the information the other person is asking about.

examples.title: Decline this time without inventing a new plan
examples.problem: You cannot meet this weekend and do not yet know another day.
steps: Thanks for inviting me. This recognizes the invitation without accepting it.
Este fin de semana no puedo.
I can’t this weekend. You do not have to offer a date you cannot keep.
Another day? This invites a later arrangement; it does not establish one now.
examples.notice: A polite response does not require an invented excuse or a promise you are not ready to make.

rescue: Think of three slots: coffee, day, time. Keep the coffee, replace Saturday with Sunday, then fill the time slot with a las once.
transfer: A friend proposes Saturday coffee. Say you cannot Saturday and suggest Sunday at eleven.
Me gustaría, pero no puedo el sábado. ¿El domingo a las once? This is one natural way to keep the invitation while changing its date.

questions.prompt: Which reply clearly changes the day without rejecting the coffee?
choices: Me gustaría, pero no puedo el sábado. ¿El domingo?
No puedo, so Saturday is agreed.
feedback: This accepts Saturday.
The interest stays, and Sunday is offered instead.
No puedo does not establish an agreement for Saturday.
questions.nudge: Would your friend know which day you are offering?

questions.prompt: What does a las once add to the plan?
feedback: A las introduces the time here.
A price would need a different expression.
This phrase does not change who is meeting.
questions.nudge: Which part of a plan is still missing after you agree on Sunday?

subject: piano
title: Give each hand a small job
scene: Hold a low C with the left hand while the right hand plays E–D–C–D. We will hear each hand alone, then put them together at the same slow tempo.
goal: Coordinate one held left-hand note with four moving right-hand notes.
needs: Find C, D and E and keep a four-beat pulse. No pedal is needed.
terms: Two Cs in different registers; C3 is one octave below C4.
A low note supplying the bottom of the sound here.
Both hands begin their first note on the same beat.
explanation: The left hand does not need a complicated part to join the music. Give it one low C and hold it while the right hand moves. In our example the left hand plays C3; the right uses C4, D4 and E4 an octave higher. The numbers locate the register. They are not finger numbers.

Count 1, 2, 3, 4. On 1, begin low C and high E together. On 2, keep the left C down and move the right hand to D. On 3, the right hand reaches C; on 4, it goes back to D. Release at the end of the fourth beat. The left hand has one attack lasting four beats; the right has four attacks. If the left hand starts copying the right-hand rhythm, stop and rehearse its single hold again.
decision: Learn the two jobs separately at the tempo you intend to use together. Then practice the first simultaneous attack. That first E over low C is the join; getting it calmly matters more than playing the whole bar quickly.

mistake.attempt: Every time the right hand changes note, press the left C again too.
mistake.diagnosis: That gives the left hand four attacks instead of the sustained bass in this example. The hands have accidentally taken the same rhythmic job.
mistake.repair: Hold the left C through the complete count while saying the right-hand notes aloud. Then add those four right-hand presses, leaving the left key down.
mistake.check: In the combined playback, listen for one low attack under four higher ones. The low note should not restart on beats 2, 3 or 4.

examples.title: One bass note under four melody notes
examples.problem: At 60 beats per minute, hold C3 for four beats while the right hand plays E4–D4–C4–D4.
steps: Use a comfortable finger. Keep the wrist relaxed; do not press harder to make the note last.
E4, D4, C4, D4: one beat each.
The thumb can stay over C4, index over D4 and middle finger over E4.
Left C3 and right E4 begin together.
Prepare both hands before starting the count.
The left hand holds; the right changes on beats 2, 3 and 4.
Release both at the end of beat 4. Slow down if the hands start copying one another.
examples.notice: Two hands do not have to play the same rhythm.

examples.title: Make the join smaller
examples.problem: Both hands work alone, but putting them together causes hesitation.
steps: Play C3 and E4 together, then release.
Practice the simultaneous start without the rest of the phrase.
Hold C3 while the right moves E4 to D4.
Now you have practiced the point at which one hand moves and the other stays.
Keep the same unhurried tempo you used for the two-note fragment.
examples.notice: Practice the difficult join, then return it to the phrase; repeated full restarts can leave the join unlearned.

rescue: Keep the left hand on the table, holding one finger down. Tap E, D, C, D with the right while counting four beats. The left hand stays still. Then transfer that feeling to the keys.
transfer: Describe what each hand does on beat 2 and how many attacks each hand makes in the four-beat example.
On beat 2 the left hand keeps holding C3 while the right changes to D4. The left has one attack; the right has four.

questions.prompt: What does the left hand do when the right moves to D4 on beat 2?
feedback: That adds an attack the sustained part does not ask for.
The bass note is meant to continue through four beats.
One sustained bass note continues under the changing melody.
questions.hint: The left-hand note lasts four beats.
questions.nudge: Which hand has moving notes in this example?

questions.prompt: The combination is hard although each hand works alone. Which smaller task addresses the join?
choices: Play faster until the hands agree.
Practice C3 and E4 starting together, then add the move to D4.
Replace the bass note with an unrelated chord.
feedback: Speed usually makes an uncertain join harder.
This isolates the simultaneous start and the first independent movement.
Adding notes changes the task before the join is secure.
questions.hint: Find where the two jobs first meet.
questions.nudge: What happens on the first beat and the next one?

subject: piano
title: Change from C major to F major without rushing
scene: A chord change is a small hand movement that has to arrive on time. Let’s place both chords, hear them, and practice the move before putting it into a steady count.
goal: Move between C–E–G and F–A–C with an even four-beat pulse.
needs: Find and play a C-major triad and count a held note or chord.
terms: F, A and C; four semitones then three above F.
Moving from one set of chord tones to the next.
The chord root is the lowest note in these two shapes.
explanation: Place your right thumb on C4, middle finger on E4 and little finger on G4. That is our C-major shape. For F major in this lesson, move the whole hand right: thumb to F4, middle finger to A4 and little finger to C5. Keep a comfortable curved hand instead of trying to leave the thumb on C while stretching the other fingers to the new notes.

First make the move without a clock. Find C–E–G, release, and find F–A–C. Once you can place both shapes, count four beats on C and four on F. Prepare to travel near the end of the hold, releasing soon enough to arrive calmly on the next 1. A small gap is fine while learning. Sustain pedal can blur a late change, so leave it out while checking the hand movement.
decision: Keep the chord names and the physical shapes connected. On each new count of 1, ask which root the thumb is finding. If the change is late, lower the tempo or rehearse the move without timing; do not squeeze the next four beats into the lost time.

mistake.attempt: I landed on F late, so I’ll play its four beats faster to catch up.
mistake.diagnosis: That changes the pulse after every difficult move. You are learning a rushed recovery instead of an even chord change.
mistake.repair: Stop, lower the tempo, and practice the release-and-land motion from C–E–G to F–A–C. Then return to four evenly spaced beats per chord.
mistake.check: Listen to the count rather than only the chord names. The beat spacing should stay the same through the change.

examples.title: Three calm chord arrivals
examples.problem: Play C major for four beats, F major for four, then C major for four. Use one right-hand chord at a time.
steps: Use thumb, middle and little finger if that is comfortable.
Find the second shape before timing it
These are the root, third and fifth of F. The hand moves to a higher position.
Give each chord a full count
Each chord starts on a new 1. The pulse does not restart more slowly or quickly because the notes changed.
The return is another transition to learn, not something to assume will work because the first direction worked.
examples.notice: Chord recognition and timely movement are separate skills; practice both.

examples.title: Rehearse the return trip
examples.problem: C to F is comfortable, but you miss E when coming back to C.
steps: Return to the whole shape, not just a familiar thumb note.
Release F–A–C and place C–E–G slowly.
Check the middle finger is on E, not F.
Hold F for four beats, then arrive on C at the next 1.
Choose a slow enough tempo that the correct movement fits.
examples.notice: A chord change has two directions. An uneven return deserves its own short rehearsal.

rescue: Make two silent hand shapes on the keys: C–E–G, then F–A–C. Do not play yet. Once both locations are clear, sound them one at a time and only then add the count.
transfer: Why should you rehearse F to C separately if C to F already works?
The reverse move has a different arrival location and can expose a different error. Practice landing on C–E–G, then place it back into the steady count.

questions.prompt: Which notes make the F-major chord used here?
feedback: F is the root, A the third and C the fifth.
These are neighboring letters, not this triad.
This does not include the third A.
questions.hint: Start at F and skip a white key twice.
questions.nudge: Where did the thumb, middle and little finger land?

questions.prompt: A late change makes you rush the following count. What should you adjust first?
choices: Press the pedal to hide it.
Slow down and rehearse the release and arrival.
feedback: Pedal does not teach the timing of the hand movement.
More chords add transitions before this one is secure.
This gives the movement time to become reliable while preserving an even pulse.
questions.hint: Make the difficult movement fit the pulse.
questions.nudge: Can you place the target shape accurately without timing it yet?

subject: chess
title: Is that piece really free to take?
scene: A bishop can capture a knight. Before taking it, look for the opponent’s reply. We will compare the same-looking capture with and without a defender.
goal: Trace a bishop capture and distinguish a free piece from a possible exchange.
needs: Recognize bishop diagonals, captures and king attacks.
terms: A piece with no other piece protecting its square in the stated position.
A capture in reply that takes the piece which just captured.
Bishop captures on f7 and gives check in the second example.
explanation: White has king g1 and bishop c4; Black has king a8 and knight f7. The bishop’s route is c4–d5–e6–f7. There is nothing on d5 or e6, so it can reach the knight. After Bxf7, the black king is far away on a8 and cannot take the bishop. In this four-piece position, White has won the knight without giving up a piece.

Now put Black’s king on g8 instead of a8. The bishop can still capture the knight on f7, and this capture gives check along the diagonal f7–g8. But Black can answer Kxf7: the king steps onto f7 and captures the bishop. White’s king on g1 does not attack f7, and there are no other white pieces in the example. The capture is now a possible exchange of bishop for knight, rather than a free knight. A defended piece is not automatically untouchable; it changes the calculation.
decision: Name the capture, place the bishop on the destination, and ask what Black can do next. That second picture is where the difference appears. A path that is clear before the move tells us the capture is possible, not whether it wins material for free.

mistake.attempt: The bishop reaches f7 in both positions, so it wins a free knight in both.
mistake.diagnosis: The movement is the same, but the defending king is not. With a king on g8, f7 can be recaptured legally in this sparse position.
mistake.repair: After Bxf7+, show Kxf7. Remove the knight, then remove the bishop. Count the actual pieces exchanged instead of stopping after White’s capture.
mistake.check: Bishops and knights are often valued at about three points each, but those values are rough guides. The specific position still determines whether a trade is useful.

examples.title: The undefended knight
examples.problem: White: Kg1, Bc4. Black: Ka8, Nf7. White to move. Can the bishop take the knight without being recaptured immediately?
steps: The bishop follows one diagonal; d5 and e6 are empty.
The knight is removed and the bishop arrives on f7.
The king on a8 cannot reach f7 in one move.
Black has no other pieces in the stated position.
White wins the knight without losing the bishop immediately.
This conclusion depends on the four pieces we named, not merely on the bishop’s movement shape.
examples.notice: Check the resulting position before calling a capture free.

examples.title: Move one defender and the conclusion changes
examples.problem: Use White Kg1, Bc4 and Black Kg8, Nf7 instead. Follow Bxf7+ and Black’s response.
steps: The bishop takes the knight and attacks the king on g8.
The king moves one diagonal square and captures the bishop. F7 is not attacked by White’s king on g1.
A bishop was exchanged for a knight.
White did not get a free knight. Whether this exchange is desirable would need more context in a fuller game.
examples.notice: Adding a defender changes what happens after the capture, even when the capturing piece has the same clear path.

rescue: Take two photographs in your mind: before White captures, and after Black replies. In the first example the bishop remains; in the second the king can take it.
transfer: Why is the knight free to take with Black’s king on a8, but not with the king on g8 in these stated positions?
A8 is too far from f7 for an immediate king recapture. From g8 the king can answer Bxf7+ with Kxf7, because the destination is not attacked by the only remaining white piece, Kg1.

questions.prompt: After Bxf7+ with Black’s king on g8, what reply must you consider?
choices: A rook move by a rook that is not on the board.
The king must ignore the check.
feedback: The king can capture the bishop on the safe adjacent square f7 in this position.
Use the actual pieces listed in the position.
Every reply must leave the king safe.
questions.hint: The king is one diagonal step from f7.
questions.nudge: Can the checking piece itself be captured?

questions.prompt: What changed between the two examples?
choices: The bishop began moving like a rook.
The bishop lost its diagonal path.
The black king could recapture on f7.
feedback: The bishop’s movement rule stayed the same.
The intermediate squares stayed empty.
Moving the king from a8 to g8 supplied a legal recapture.
questions.nudge: Which piece changed its square between the examples?

subject: chess
title: Play an opening with a reason for each move
scene: Start from the ordinary initial position. Instead of memorizing a string of letters, watch how pawn moves make room and the small pieces enter the game.
goal: Explain the jobs of e4, Nf3 and Bc4, and adjust when Black chooses a different center move.
needs: Know the piece movements and recognize check. This is one legal opening example, not a compulsory script.
terms: Bringing pieces from their starting squares into useful play.
The central squares, especially d4, e4, d5 and e5.
The dots show Black’s move in the written line.
The pawn from the e-file captures on d5.
explanation: On the starting board, White’s bishop on f1 is shut in by its own pawns. Moving the e-pawn from e2 to e4 opens the diagonal through e2 and also puts a pawn in the center. After Black answers e5, White can develop the knight from g1 to f3. That knight attacks the pawn on e5. Black’s Nc6 both develops a knight and protects that pawn.

White’s Bc4 then uses the diagonal the first pawn move opened: f1–e2–d3–c4. The bishop points toward f7, but that pawn is protected by Black’s king. Looking at a target does not mean taking it would win something. Black can develop with Bc5. These moves put pieces to work; they are not a guarantee of an advantage. If Black plays a different move, inspect what changed instead of forcing the remembered sequence onto a new position.
decision: For each move, name a job you can see on the board: occupy the center, open a path, develop a piece, or answer a threat. Then check the opponent’s last move. A familiar move is useful only if it still fits the position.

mistake.attempt: I learned e4, Nf3, Bc4, so I should always play them without looking at Black’s replies.
mistake.diagnosis: Black’s moves can change the pawn structure and create threats. Memorizing only White’s half of an opening misses those changes.
mistake.repair: Compare 1 e4 e5 with 1 e4 d5. In the second line, the pawn on d5 directly attacks e4. One legal continuation is exd5 Qxd5 Nc3, with the knight then attacking the queen.
mistake.check: Describe what the opponent just attacked or opened before choosing your next move. An opening principle helps you think; it does not replace inspecting the board.

examples.title: Open a path, then use it
examples.problem: Follow 1 e4 e5 2 Nf3 Nc6 3 Bc4 Bc5 from the starting position.
steps: Both e-pawns advance two squares from their starting rank. Their bishops now have open diagonals.
The knight leaves g1 and attacks e5 from f3.
The black knight leaves b8 and protects the e5 pawn.
Each bishop moves out through the square its e-pawn vacated. Both sides have begun development; the game is still open.
examples.notice: The first pawn moves and later bishop moves are connected. Remembering that connection is more useful than reciting the letters alone.

examples.title: Black chooses a different center move
examples.problem: After 1 e4, Black plays d5. Follow one legal response and explain the next threat.
steps: Black’s pawn on d5 attacks White’s pawn on e4.
White’s e-pawn captures on d5. Black’s queen comes down the cleared d-file to recapture.
The knight on c3 attacks d5. Black must consider the threat to the queen when replying.
examples.notice: Different pawn contact produces a different worked line. This example illustrates adaptation, not a claim that every other move is wrong.

rescue: Watch only the e-pawn and f1 bishop first. The pawn moves away; the bishop’s door opens. Then watch the two knights: f3 attacks e5, and c6 protects e5.
transfer: Explain how 1 e4 helps White’s bishop, and why Black’s d5 deserves attention before following a memorized plan.
E4 vacates e2 and opens the f1 bishop’s diagonal. A black pawn on d5 attacks e4, so White should inspect that contact and possible replies rather than ignore Black’s move.

questions.prompt: What does 1 e4 do for the bishop on f1?
choices: It opens the diagonal through e2.
It lets the bishop jump over pawns.
feedback: The pawn leaves e2 rather than adding a blocker.
The bishop can later travel through the square the pawn vacated.
Bishops still cannot jump.
questions.hint: Look at the square the pawn leaves.
questions.nudge: Which square was immediately in the bishop’s way?

questions.prompt: In 1 e4 d5 2 exd5 Qxd5 3 Nc3, what does the knight on c3 attack?
feedback: C3 to d5 is a two-and-one knight offset.
E8 is not a knight destination from c3.
H8 is far outside the knight’s reach from c3.
questions.hint: Count the knight offset from c3.
questions.nudge: Which black piece just arrived on d5?
